topic: Feature Store Skew: When Training Data Lies to Production
postText:
Model hit 0.94 AUC in the notebook. In production, it scored 0.61. Same model. Same weights. Same code path. So what broke?

The feature pipeline. Training read from a batch warehouse table. Serving read from a Redis cache fed by a streaming job. Two pipelines, two definitions of the same feature, two different answers. Nobody caught it for three weeks because the dashboard only tracked latency, not prediction quality.

This is feature skew. It's the silent killer of ML in production, and it's more common than model drift.

What we changed:

1. Single feature definition. One source of truth for each feature, consumed by both training and serving. No duplicate transformation logic living in two codebases.

2. Log the feature vector at inference time. Persist the exact inputs that produced each prediction. Without this, you cannot debug a bad prediction. You are guessing.

3. Skew detection in CI. Compare offline vs online feature statistics on every deploy. Fail the build if the distribution gap crosses a threshold. Cheaper than discovering it from users.

Lesson from healthcare IT: a model that predicts no-shows or readmission risk is only as good as the features it sees at inference. If those features are computed differently in the warehouse versus the serving layer, the model is confidently wrong. In a clinical context, confidently wrong is worse than silent.

The hard part was never the model. It was keeping the data contract honest across two systems that evolved independently.

Question for the ML engineers here: how do you detect feature skew in your stack today? Offline replay, statistical monitoring, or do you only find out when business metrics drop?

Like this if it hit close to home. Comment your approach below. Share with your data and platform teams who own the feature pipeline.
